title: AI Can Drive Social Impact. Here’s How.
gist: BCG argues that in low- and middle-income countries the AI model itself accounts for only ~10% of what determines whether an AI service scales, compute and data ~20%, and people, processes and ecosystem ~70% — so capital should be aimed at binding constraints like delivery channels, builder talent and policy rather than at better models. It points to Rajasthan's 3.5-million-student AI education program, Telangana's Data Exchange, and India's hyperscaler compute partnerships as working entry points.

insights.claim: BCG proposes a 10:20:70 rule of thumb for AI deployment in developing markets: the model accounts for roughly 10% of what determines success, compute and data another 20%, and people, processes, and the surrounding ecosystem roughly 70%.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: If 70% of value creation sits outside the model layer, the durable margin in AI-for-development sits with systems integrators, delivery operators and data/infrastructure vendors rather than model providers.
insights.quote: the model itself may account for only around 10% of what determines success, compute and data for another 20%, and people, processes, and the surrounding ecosystem for roughly 70%
insights.locator: Look Beyond the AI Model — "The relative importance of these layers"

insights.claim: Investment and attention in AI-for-development flow disproportionately to the technology layer, which is the inverse of where the determinants of success actually sit.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Signals a persistent capital misallocation — the underfunded layers (delivery, talent, local data) are where scarce assets and pricing power will accumulate.
insights.quote: Investment and attention, however, often gravitate toward the most visible part of the house: the technology.
insights.locator: Look Beyond the AI Model — "Investment and attention, however"

insights.claim: Population-scale AI impact is framed as requiring eight essential elements: national or regional strategy and orchestration at the top, then models and applications, accessible compute, relevant high-quality local and domain data, fit-for-purpose capital, builder talent, sustainable delivery channels, and deep understanding of how intended users live and decide.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: A checklist for screening AI-for-development deals: ventures missing delivery channels or durable capital are pilot-stage regardless of model quality.
insights.locator: Look Beyond the AI Model — "Population-scale AI impact requires eight essential elements"

insights.claim: A technically excellent AI application can still fail outright if it lacks a supporting policy framework, sufficient local talent to adapt it, a viable route to users, or durable funding after the pilot ends.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Model accuracy is a poor predictor of commercial survival in these markets — diligence should weight distribution and budget-line integration far higher.
insights.quote: A working AI model does not automatically create a working AI service.
insights.locator: Opening — "A working AI model does not automatically"

insights.claim: The strategic question for funders is reframed from how to build better AI to how to create the conditions in which useful AI can survive and scale.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Development-finance and philanthropic AI budgets may rotate away from model grants toward infrastructure, talent and delivery — watch where DFI mandates land.
insights.locator: Look Beyond the AI Model — "The question for governments, development institutions"

insights.claim: There is no universal playbook for scaling AI in low- and middle-income countries because countries start from structurally different positions — one may have strong digital infrastructure but fragmented government leadership, another political commitment and funding but poor-quality local data, a third data and technical capability but no delivery channels to reach users.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Country-level AI opportunity cannot be indexed generically; each market needs a constraint-specific thesis before capital is committed.
insights.locator: Find the Binding Constraints — "There is no universal playbook"

insights.claim: In environments constrained by capacity, capability and cash, strengthening every ecosystem element simultaneously is described as neither realistic nor efficient; leaders should instead identify the single binding constraint currently preventing the ecosystem from delivering impact.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Concentrated, sequenced interventions beat broad programs — favor operators with an explicit constraint diagnosis over those pitching full-stack national AI plans.
insights.quote: That changes the strategic question from “What AI should we build?” to “What is preventing AI from scaling here?”
insights.locator: Find the Binding Constraints — "In environments constrained by capacity"

insights.claim: The 10:20:70 framework explicitly does not make compute and data secondary — in some contexts they are hard prerequisites, such as a regulated service requiring local compute that does not yet exist or an application depending on digital public infrastructure it must interface with.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Data-residency and regulated-workload rules create a floor of local compute demand independent of model economics — relevant for regional datacenter buildouts.
insights.locator: Find the Binding Constraints — "Nor does the 10:20:70 framework imply"

insights.claim: Building data infrastructure without sufficient usable data or without creating demand for its use simply produces an expensive stranded asset.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: A warning on national data-platform capex: utilization, not construction, is the metric that determines whether these projects generate returns.
insights.quote: Building data infrastructure without sufficient or usable data—or without creating demand for its use—may simply create an expensive asset.
insights.locator: Find the Binding Constraints — "Building data infrastructure without"

insights.claim: Rwanda's national AI roadmap work is cited as the model for constraint-led sequencing: assess the wider system, inventory existing capabilities and infrastructure, determine what is holding progress back, and sequence interventions accordingly rather than funding a collection of individual technology projects.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Rwanda is positioned as a reference implementation other African national AI strategies may copy — an early indicator of where donor and vendor flows go next.
insights.locator: Find the Binding Constraints — "National AI roadmap work in countries such as Rwanda"

insights.claim: Three broad entry points are identified for starting population-scale AI: national AI strategy, policy and orchestration; high-impact solution delivery that builds outward; and essential-element activation targeting a foundational constraint such as data, compute, capital or talent.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Gives a taxonomy for classifying government AI programs and anticipating which vendor category — advisory, application, or infrastructure — captures the initial spend.
insights.locator: Choose the Right Door to Scale — "In practice, there are three broad ways to begin"

insights.claim: Where AI activity is fragmented across government, donors, technology providers and other institutions, the binding constraint is diagnosed as the absence of common direction, making national strategies and orchestration mechanisms the highest-leverage first move.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Fragmented-donor markets are early-stage; expect advisory and roadmap mandates to precede any material technology procurement there.
insights.locator: Choose the Right Door to Scale — "National AI Strategy, Policy, and Orchestration"

insights.claim: A single demonstrated high-impact AI solution can act as a focal point around which funding, institutional support, talent and delivery capacity coalesce.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: One flagship win can unlock a whole national budget line — track lighthouse deployments as leading indicators of follow-on procurement.
insights.locator: Choose the Right Door to Scale — "High-Impact Solution Delivery and Building Outward"

insights.claim: An AI-enabled education program in Rajasthan, India — repeated student assessment, AI identification of individual learning gaps, personalized remediation recommendations, and teachers equipped to act on the insights — reached approximately 3.5 million children.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that adaptive-learning AI can reach millions of students in a low-resource public system, validating state-level edtech as an addressable market.
insights.locator: Choose the Right Door to Scale — "In Rajasthan, India, for example"

insights.claim: The Rajasthan AI education program produced a 10%–12% stabilized year-over-year reduction in the number of children two or more grades behind.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: A rare quantified outcome metric for AI in public education — the benchmark competing programs and procurement bids will be measured against.
insights.quote: a 10%–12% stabilized year-over-year reduction in children two or more grades behind
insights.locator: Choose the Right Door to Scale — "The program reached approximately 3.5 million kids"

insights.claim: The Rajasthan program's success is attributed less to the technology than to its embedding in leadership priorities, assessment cycles, teacher routines, budgets and policy, plus coordination among parents, teachers and policymakers.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Adoption engineering, not model quality, is the replicable moat — favor vendors with institutional change-management capability over pure-tech providers.
insights.quote: Success depended not just on technology itself but on how it was adopted.
insights.locator: Choose the Right Door to Scale — "Success depended not just on technology"

insights.claim: Telangana's Data Exchange, designed and built with BCG, combines public and private data, pre-trained models, curated use cases, compute and a development sandbox, and engaged more than 200 stakeholders across over 50 entities including state data providers, incubators, startups and investors.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: A template for state-level data-marketplace infrastructure; participation counts show whether such exchanges generate real developer demand or remain stranded assets.
insights.locator: Essential-Element Activation — "In Telangana, India, BCG helped design"

insights.claim: The Telangana AI Rising Grand Challenge attracted more than 420 applications from over 240 startups, with six winners selected to deliver solutions with government departments spanning transport, education and health.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Concrete measure of India's state-level AI startup supply — a pipeline worth screening for early-stage exposure to public-sector AI deployment.
insights.locator: Essential-Element Activation — "The Telangana AI Rising Grand Challenge"

insights.claim: India is expanding access to local compute through partnerships with hyperscalers and AI service providers, combined with structured pricing and major investment in digital public infrastructure, and attention is described as now shifting toward the people, process and ecosystem factors that make up the remaining 70%.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: India has cleared the compute and DPI prerequisite stage, so the next wave of spend there should favor application, delivery and integration players over infrastructure.
insights.locator: Essential-Element Activation — "India is showing how to address constraints"

insights.claim: Funding pilots without a pathway into government budgets and institutional routines produces impressive demonstrations that disappear when the funding does.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Revenue durability in gov-tech AI depends on budget-line conversion — a pilot-heavy revenue mix is a red flag for recurring revenue quality.
insights.quote: Funding pilots without a pathway into government budgets and institutional routines can produce impressive demonstrations that disappear when the funding does.
insights.locator: Find the Binding Constraints — "Funding pilots without a pathway"

insights.claim: The ultimate test for an AI service in development contexts is whether it becomes part of the system — supported by policy, incorporated into budgets, integrated into institutional routines, maintained locally, and delivered repeatedly — rather than whether it works during a demonstration or grant period.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Defines the KPI that separates one-off grant revenue from annuity-like public contracts in this sector.
insights.locator: Build for Permanence, Not Pilots — "For governments and development institutions"

insights.claim: AI ecosystem development in these markets is described as self-reinforcing: a coherent national strategy attracts investment and talent, better local data access lowers application development cost, a successful population-scale use case strengthens political support and unlocks funding, and trusted delivery channels built for one service can subsequently carry others.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Implies increasing returns and winner-take-more dynamics at the country level — early-mover markets like India and Rwanda may compound their lead.
insights.locator: Build for Permanence, Not Pilots — "A coherent national strategy can attract investment"

insights.claim: The architecture of the AI economy is being built now, and whether low- and middle-income countries benefit will depend not on access to the most powerful technology but on whether governments, funders, technology partners and local actors can orchestrate ecosystems around their own priorities.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Frames a closing window: the distribution of AI economic gains across emerging markets is being set in the current investment cycle, not later.
insights.quote: The architecture of the AI economy is being built now.
insights.locator: Build for Permanence, Not Pilots — "For low- and middle-income countries, the stakes"

insights.claim: A 2030 scenario is sketched in which AI gains are widespread: a smallholder farmer gets planting advice tuned to local soil conditions and the week's rain forecast, a child in a resource-constrained classroom receives native-language tutoring tailored to his pace, and a community health worker backed by an AI-native ministry spots warning signs of illness in a newborn before the family travels to a clinic.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Names the three end-markets — agri-advisory, vernacular tutoring, frontline health triage — where population-scale AI demand is expected to materialize by 2030.
insights.locator: Build for Permanence, Not Pilots — "Imagine a 2030 scenario"

insights.claim: Voice interfaces can make digital services accessible to people who cannot read or write, local-language models can reach communities global digital platforms have struggled to serve, and image-based AI can extend health care and agriculture expertise where doctors and agricultural advisers are scarce.
insights.speaker: Jim Larson
insights.so_what: Identifies the three specific AI modalities that unlock previously unreachable populations — the technical wedge for emerging-market AI TAM expansion.
insights.locator: Opening — "AI has the potential to overcome barriers"
